headline: Energy giants face growing hostile territory: political maneuvers threaten to reshape the power map
snippet: Kyrgyzstan's President Sadyr Japarov has threatened to nationalize Gazprom's gas transmission network, a move that highlights the growing friction between political demands and physical infrastructure limits in the region's energy sector. While Bishkek cites slow progress in connecting new residential and energy objects to the grid, the core constraint is not a lack of Russian intent but the physical capacity of the transit pipeline running through Kazakhstan. Infrastructure Bottlenecks and Transit Limits The dispute in Kyrgyzstan centers on the unfulfilled promise to gasify the entire republic. Japarov referenced the precedent of the Kumtor gold mine nationalization, signaling a potential similar outcome for Gazprom. Mayors and local officials, including Bishkek Mayor Aibek Djunushaliev, have echoed the criticism regarding the pace of network expansion. However, the physical reality of the energy system dictates a different timeline. Over the past decade, Kyrgyzstan's gasification rate has nearly doubled, rising from 22% to 40%. Further expansion is currently limited by the "bottleneck" effect in the transit system. During the previous winter, the pipeline segment within Kazakhstan operated at 115% of its capacity. Increasing supply volumes depends on the completion of the second line of the Beyneu-Bozoy-Shymkent pipeline. This project is being developed by Kazakhstan's QazaqGaz and Qatar's UCC Holding, not by Russian entities, meaning the constraint is external to Gazprom's direct control.

Third-Generation Nissan Pathfinder: 350,000 km Potential vs. Main Bearing Risks
snippet: For a buyer targeting a body-on-frame SUV with up to 250,000 kilometers on the clock and a budget between 1.5 and 2 million rubles, the third-generation Nissan Pathfinder presents a compelling, if cautious, proposition. Measuring 4,813 mm in length with a ground clearance of 228 mm and offering 515 liters of cargo space, the vehicle occupies a niche of practical, capable 4x4 transport. It offers a robust structural foundation and proven mechanical longevity, provided the owner is prepared to accept specific maintenance risks. The core value of this vehicle lies in its diesel powertrain and classic frame-based durability. Post-2010 models are equipped with two engine options: a 2.5-liter unit producing 190 hp and a 3.0-liter unit delivering 231 hp. Industry assessments suggest both engines are capable of reaching 350,000 to 400,000 kilometers. However, this "reserve” capacity is not merely a matter of distance; it is contingent on vigilant maintenance. The appeal is not just in the initial purchase price, but in the potential to extract significant service life from a mechanically sound machine, a trade-off that rewards the diligent and penalizes the negligent. Ownership costs and mechanical vulnerabilities The decision to purchase a specific example should be governed less by the sticker price and more by the anticipated cost of ownership. The 3.0-liter engine, while more powerful, demands particular attention. It is prone to early clogging of the EGR system and experiences wear in the camshaft chain roughly every 100,000 kilometers. More critically, there is a known risk of main bearing failure, a condition that transforms a routine service event into a prohibitively expensive major repair. The smaller 2.5-liter engine, sometimes paired with a manual transmission, offers greater gearbox longevity, though the clutch itself is a weak point.

headline: Dolphin gets a Columns view again
snippet: I am happy to announce that Dolphin has a new view mode: Columns. Each column shows one folder. Select a folder and its content opens in the next column, so the path from the folder you opened down to your selection stays on screen. This layout is known as Miller columns, after Mark S. Miller, who created it in 1980. It is now in the master branch of Dolphin, not yet in Dolphin 26.12. We can still bring it into 26.12 until November 12th, if the testers find it ready. Otherwise it will ship in Dolphin 27.04. Either way it needs testers, so read on. A bit of history Dolphin had a column view from KDE 4.0, built on Qt's QColumnView. When Peter Penz moved the views to the new KItemViews engine for Dolphin 2.0 in 2011, the column view was not ported, and it was gone. Bug 387455, "Column view in Dolphin", was opened in 2017. With 32 people in CC, it has been one of the most requested features. It is now closed. Sebastian's start In February 2026 Sebastian Englbrecht opened MR !1185, a first Miller columns view built on KItemViews. After a few weeks of review he handed it over to me, and I continued it until MR !1524 was merged. He wrote: Yeah, thank you very much meven for taking this to and over the finish line. I came to my limits and wouldn't have been able to polish it this well. Thank you Sebastian, without your first version this would not exist. What it does The folder that you open is the first column. Up, Back and the breadcrumb add its parent in front. A folder or an archive that you select opens the next column. Left, Right and Return move between the columns. The location bar, the window title, New Folder, Paste and the terminal panel follow the last column. Columns fit their content by default, or use a fixed width. Drag a handle to resize a column, double click it to fit the columns. Sort, grouping, hidden files, zoom and previews apply to every column, and a restored session brings back the open columns. Ctrl+4 switches to the mode, and Settings > View > Columns has its options. The Columns mode is in the Dolphin application only for now. Konqueror and other apps that embed Dolphin's file view do not offer it yet. The testers The view behaves the way it does because people tried it and told us what was wrong, in more than 600 comments. Lluc Pallejà tested nearly every interaction and filed over a hundred comments with screencasts. Nate Graham did the UX review. Roke Julian Lockhart Beedell, Alexander Wilms, Karol, Kai Uwe Broulik, Leopold Luley, Akseli Lahtinen, Felix Ernst, Blenux, Ke, Linux ForAll and others found bugs and argued the details. Kudos to all of you. Please test it Whether the view goes into Dolphin 26.12 is decided on November 12th, see the KDE Gear 26.12 schedule. Until then, it needs people using it on their own folders, with their own habits. On Arch Linux, the dolphin-git package from the AUR builds Dolphin from master. On any distribution, kde-builder can build it: kde-builder dolphin kde-builder --run dolphin If your distribution ships a recent KDE Frameworks, as Arch Linux or Fedora do, add --no-include-dependencies to build Dolphin alone. Then switch to Columns with Ctrl+4. Try your daily navigation, the keyboard, long names, large or remote folders, drag and drop, and resizing the window. Tell us also how it feels that the first column is the folder that you opened, as reviewers disagreed on this. Please report bugs in the view-engine: columns mode component of Dolphin, with the steps and a screenshot or screencast when you can. General impressions are welcome in the comments of this post. That's all, folks.
